title: Markets brace for a short, data-heavy week after correction
dek: US markets are closed for the weekend after Friday's AI-led selloff pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction. Futures reopen Sunday at 6 p.m. ET, and Wednesday's GDP and PCE inflation data are the last big test before the Fed's December meeting and the Thanksgiving break.
quick: Sunday edition: no US trading today. Friday left the S&P 500 at 6,910, down 3.7%, the Nasdaq down 5.3% and the VIX near 36.
Two more tankers were reported struck near Oman's Khasab on Saturday, keeping shipping risk around the Strait of Hormuz in focus for oil.
Bitcoin steadied near $59,000 Sunday morning after briefly falling to about $55,100 on Saturday; ether sits around $1,650.
Rate futures still price roughly a 90% chance of a quarter-point Fed hike on December 9, despite the stock slide.
Monday brings flash PMI surveys and remarks from New York Fed President John Williams; Agilent and Zoom report after the close.
Wednesday is the big day: Q3 GDP, October PCE inflation, jobless claims and durable goods all at 8:30 a.m. ET. Markets close Thursday.

blocks.head: Stocks head into the holiday week in correction territory
blocks.what: Friday's selloff left the S&P 500 at 6,910.39, down 3.7% on the day, and the Dow at 48,147.33, down 1.9%. Both closed more than 10% below their records, the usual definition of a correction, according to Reuters and CNBC. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% to 22,617.73 and gave up its gain for 2026. Index futures settled Friday with similar losses, and the VIX volatility gauge ended near 35.9.
blocks.why: A VIX in the mid-30s signals that options traders expect large daily swings to continue. Holiday weeks tend to have lighter trading volume, which can magnify moves in either direction, especially for the large tech and chip stocks that led the decline.
blocks.watch: Where stock futures open Sunday at 6 p.m. ET, and whether Asian chip stocks steady or keep falling Monday.

blocks.head: Nvidia's leadership turmoil and regulatory scrutiny remain the market's biggest overhang
blocks.what: Nvidia fell about 14% Friday, capping its longest weekly losing streak since 2008, per CNBC. The Wall Street Journal first reported that the SEC has opened a civil inquiry into whether the company's disclosures misled investors, and The New York Times reported the probe covers accounting practices; neither the SEC nor Nvidia has confirmed it. Weekend reporting by the Times and the Journal focused on alleged efforts to move Nvidia chips to China involving associates of Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO on November 12. Nvidia's board, led by chair Harvey Jones, has said it does not plan to reinstate him, even though President Trump has said publicly he would not mind seeing Huang return.
blocks.why: Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, and its suppliers make up a big share of markets in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan. Any new disclosure, filing or leadership news can swing chip stocks and the broader indexes.
blocks.watch: Any formal company statement on the SEC inquiry or the CEO search, and chip-stock trading in Asia Monday.

blocks.head: Wednesday's GDP and PCE data are the last major inputs before the Fed decides
blocks.what: The government will release its second estimate of third-quarter GDP and October personal income, spending and PCE inflation together Wednesday at 8:30 a.m. ET, along with weekly jobless claims and durable goods orders. Forecasts compiled in the app's calendar call for GDP growth of 3.5% annualized, up from 3.4% in the first estimate, and a 0.3% monthly rise in core PCE prices, matching the prior month. Some previews put the annual core PCE rate around 3.1% to 3.2%.
blocks.why: PCE is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. A hotter-than-expected reading could revive talk of a larger December hike and push Treasury yields higher, while a softer one could give some relief to rate-sensitive stocks and bonds.
blocks.watch: The Fed's Beige Book survey of regional business conditions, also due Wednesday afternoon.

blocks.head: More tanker strikes near the Strait of Hormuz
blocks.what: The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported two separate incidents Saturday involving outbound tankers near Khasab, Oman, at the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters and other outlets. One vessel was hit on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab and another in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east, both by unidentified projectiles; it was not clear whether the same ship was involved, and no casualties were reported. The incidents followed a similar attack Friday that caused a fire aboard a tanker, and Iran said a separate vessel struck a mine east of Hormuz, per Reuters. Shipping through the strait has been disrupted since the conflict involving Iran began on February 28.
blocks.why: The strait normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil supply, so new attacks can lift crude prices, tanker rates and insurance costs, and support energy stocks. Oil has still fallen for three straight weeks as traders focus on ample global supply.
blocks.watch: Brent and WTI when energy futures reopen Sunday evening.

blocks.head: CrowdStrike–Zscaler talks and the data-center tax threat hang over tech
blocks.what: Bloomberg and Reuters reported Friday that CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, which was valued at about $32 billion; no terms have been disclosed and the talks could end without a deal. Zscaler rose about 17% after hours while CrowdStrike fell about 8%. Separately, President Trump said Friday he would impose a large tax on US companies that build AI data centers abroad, without giving details on size, timing or legal basis, according to NBC News and The New York Times.
blocks.why: A deal would be among the largest in cybersecurity and could lift other security software stocks on takeover hopes. The tax remark adds uncertainty for the big cloud companies with overseas data-center plans, though tax policy requires action by Congress.
blocks.watch: Whether either company confirms the talks before Monday's open, and any written proposal on the data-center tax.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets are closed for the weekend and reopen Sunday evening US time. On Friday, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell about 5.1% to 56,437, South Korea's KOSPI dropped about 5.2% and Taiwan's main index lost about 6.2%, capping its worst week since 1991, according to Reuters. Chinese markets fell less: the Hang Seng slipped 1.9% and Shanghai 1.2%. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 8.3% for the week, its worst since March 2020, per Reuters. Chip-heavy markets took the brunt because their companies supply Nvidia and other AI hardware buyers. In weekend news, South Korea's education minister resigned, per the BBC, The New York Times and The Guardian, a domestic political story with no direct market link.
Europe

The Stoxx 600 fell 2.0% Friday to 625.65, its fifth straight decline and its worst week since March, down about 5.8%. Germany's DAX lost 2.6% and the UK's FTSE 100 about 1.0%, with chip-equipment makers ASML and STMicroelectronics down more than 9%, per Reuters. CNBC reported that an early breakdown in the polar vortex could bring colder, less windy weather to Europe, straining a gas market where storage began the winter at its lowest level in more than a decade. That is a risk to watch for European utilities and industrial companies.
Currencies

Currency markets are shut until Sunday evening, so these are Friday's closing levels. The yen was the week's main safe haven: the dollar fell about 0.7% Friday to roughly 158.5 yen, moving away from the 160 level traders watch for possible Japanese intervention. The dollar index finished near 103.8, little changed, after hitting its highest in about 19 months earlier Friday on Fed hike expectations, per CNBC. The euro was flat near $1.097, the pound near $1.308, and the dollar edged up to about 6.68 yuan.

US stocks and futures are closed for the weekend, so the table below shows Friday's final levels. S&P 500 futures ended down about 3.2%, Nasdaq 100 futures down nearly 5% and Dow futures down about 1.6%, in line with the cash indexes. Small caps held up somewhat better: the Russell 2000 fell 2.8%, less than the Nasdaq, because the selling centered on large tech and chip stocks.

The first read on Monday's open comes when futures resume trading Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. Weekend items that could move them include the Hormuz tanker incidents, any news on Nvidia or the CrowdStrike–Zscaler talks, and the tone of Asian trading in chip stocks.

Treasurys rallied Friday as investors moved money out of stocks. The 2-year yield, which tracks Fed expectations most closely, fell about 13 basis points to 4.65%. The 10-year dropped about 10 basis points to 4.95%, and the 30-year slipped about 6 basis points to 5.34%. Because short-term yields fell more than long-term ones, the curve steepened slightly: the 10-year now yields about 30 basis points more than the 2-year.

The bond rally reflected demand for safety, not a shift in Fed expectations. Fed funds futures priced about a 90% chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting late last week, with most of the remainder on a half-point move, according to CME FedWatch data cited by several outlets. Reports citing the same data show traders see roughly even odds of another hike in January. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has argued for considering a half-point move, while New York Fed President John Williams has said conditions do not call for dramatic action. Governor Lisa Cook has said further increases are needed, and minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expected a December hike.
Fed speakers

items: Monday: New York Fed President John Williams, a permanent voter on rates, is scheduled to speak in the afternoon ET, per the app's calendar.
Wednesday: the Beige Book is released at 2 p.m. ET. Fed officials enter their pre-meeting quiet period on Saturday, November 28.

blocks.text: Sectors

Technology was by far the weakest S&P 500 sector Friday, down about 7.3% as chipmakers sold off. Industrials (down 3.1%), consumer discretionary (down 3.0%), communication services (down 2.7%) and materials (down 2.2%) also lagged, all groups tied to AI spending or to megacap tech. Consumer staples was the only sector to rise, up about 0.7%, while health care was nearly flat and utilities, energy and real estate fell less than 1%. CNBC noted that long-unpopular defensive names such as Clorox and Campbell's have been gaining as the AI trade loses steam, a sign of investors rotating toward steady earners.
Names to watch Monday

items: Nvidia: down about 14% Friday; weekend coverage of the chip-smuggling case and the reported SEC inquiry keeps it in focus.
Micron and AMD: each fell about 13% to 14% Friday in the chip selloff.
Anthropic: ended Friday near $89, down about 8.5% in its second trading day and close to its $83 IPO price.
Zscaler and CrowdStrike: up about 17% and down about 8% after hours, respectively, on the reported takeover talks.
Procter & Gamble: The New York Times reported the company runs 15 sites that can operate factory shifts without workers on site and plans to add more in 2027 to cut costs.
Agilent, Zoom and Workday: scheduled to report after Monday's close.

blocks.text: Oil

WTI crude settled Friday at $83.98 a barrel and Brent at $92.57, both up modestly on the day but down for a third straight week, with WTI off 5.2% and Brent 3.4% for the week. Traders have been weighing steady global supply against repeated attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Saturday's two new tanker incidents near Khasab add to that risk when futures reopen Sunday evening.
Gold

Gold fell about 4% Friday to near $3,539 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025. Expectations of more Fed hikes and a firm dollar raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest, and some investors sold gold to cover losses elsewhere, so it has not acted as a haven in this selloff.
Crypto

Bitcoin, which trades around the clock, was near $59,000 early Sunday, up about 2% over 24 hours but down about 8% over seven days, according to CoinGecko data reported by crypto outlets. It briefly fell to about $55,100 on Saturday, its lowest since 2024, before rebounding. Ether traded around $1,650 to $1,670. Analysts cited outflows from crypto ETFs and the broader retreat from risk; the Crypto Fear & Greed Index has sat in extreme fear all week. The app's quote table may show slightly older figures.
There are no US economic releases on Sunday. The items that matter most for the start of the week:

items: Sunday, 6 p.m. ET: US stock, bond and oil futures reopen.
Monday, 9:45 a.m. ET: S&P Global flash PMIs for November. Forecasts call for manufacturing at 54.5, down from 56.0, and services at 55.6, down from 57.9. Readings above 50 signal expansion.
Monday afternoon: New York Fed President John Williams speaks.
Tuesday, 10 a.m. ET: Conference Board consumer confidence, forecast at 92.1 versus 91.7, a read on holiday spending.
Wednesday, 8:30 a.m. ET: Q3 GDP (forecast 3.5%), October core PCE (forecast 0.3% monthly), jobless claims (forecast 201,000) and durable goods.

blocks.text: No major companies report on Sunday. These are the key scheduled reports for the start of the week; dates come from company announcements and earnings calendars, and a few may still shift.

rows: Lab-equipment demand from drug and research customers; consensus near $1.73 a share.
Enterprise growth and AI features; estimates range from about $1.39 to $1.49 a share.
Subscription growth and whether AI is helping or hurting demand for business software.
Industrial and auto chip orders; a read on chip demand outside AI after Friday's rout.
Holiday outlook and electronics demand heading into Black Friday.
AI server sales and backlog, a direct test of AI spending; consensus about $6.62 a share.
PC demand and memory-chip cost pressures.

blocks.text: It is a holiday-shortened week: US stock markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday, with bond markets also closing early. Monday's flash PMIs and Williams' remarks open the week, Dell's results Tuesday evening are the main test of AI hardware spending after the chip selloff, and Wednesday packs GDP, PCE inflation, durable goods, jobless claims and the Beige Book into one day before the break. Friday's Black Friday sales give the first read on holiday demand. With volatility high and trading volume usually thin around Thanksgiving, news on Nvidia, the Fed or the Strait of Hormuz could move prices more than usual.

bottom_line: Markets enter Thanksgiving week in correction after the sharpest AI-led selloff in years, with volatility elevated and a December Fed hike still largely priced in. Wednesday's inflation and growth data are the main scheduled catalyst before the holiday.
